planting.note: Plant offsets or rooted rosettes in spring into sharply drained, gritty soil in full sun.

directions: Sempervivum heuffelii is the wild Balkan species behind the many large, clumping, jewel-toned named cultivars already popular in rock gardens, distinguished from other hens and chicks by rosettes that stay intact rather than producing separate chicks on stolons. In its plain form it carries broad green to bronze-tinted leaves that color up with cold and stress, slowly dividing to form a tight mound. Grow it in full sun on sharply drained, mineral-rich soil, such as a gravel bed, trough, or rock garden, and avoid any soil that holds moisture around the crown. It is extremely drought tolerant and essentially maintenance-free once established, needing only occasional division when clumps become congested.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Seed in early fall or early spring into well-prepared soil; this fine-leaved fescue establishes slowly but tolerates low mowing and minimal fertility once rooted.

directions: Hard fescue is the wild fine-fescue species behind many low-input, shade-tolerant turf cultivars already bred for lawns and no-mow meadows, forming dense, fine-textured, bluish-green tufts. It tolerates infertile, droughty soil and both deep shade and full sun better than most turf grasses, needing little water or fertilizer once established. Sow seed in early fall for best establishment, or in early spring as a second choice, and mow infrequently and high to maintain its naturally tufted look. It is a durable, low-maintenance choice for banks, roadsides, and naturalized no-mow areas.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into well-drained soil, and set a male pollinator nearby since most female seedlings need one to fruit well.

directions: Che, also called mandarin melon berry, is the East Asian wild-type species behind the several named male and female selections already grown for fruit production, producing round, raspberry-like red fruit with a sweet, mild melon flavor on female trees. It is closely related to mulberry and Osage orange and shares their toughness, tolerating heat, drought, and poor soil once established. Plant in full sun on well-drained soil, and because most seedling females need a separate male pollinator to set fruit, plan for at least one of each if growing from unselected seedling stock. It bears some scattered thorns on young wood, which lessen as the tree matures.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or fall into well-drained soil in full sun; this species is almost always propagated from cuttings rather than seed.

directions: Flaky juniper is the Himalayan species behind many low, spreading or compact blue-foliaged garden junipers already popular as groundcovers and dwarf specimens, bearing densely packed, overlapping scale-like needles. In its wild form it ranges from a sprawling groundcover to a small, irregular shrub or tree depending on provenance and growing conditions. Plant in full sun on well-drained soil; it dislikes wet feet and is intolerant of standing water or heavy, poorly drained clay. Once established it is drought-tolerant and needs only occasional shaping, since its naturally irregular, picturesque form is part of its appeal.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or small plugs after frost danger passes into consistently moist, well-drained soil or a hanging basket.

directions: Bacopa is the South African wild-type species behind the dozens of named trailing bedding and basket cultivars already sold under brand names, bearing small five-petaled white flowers scattered over a mounding, trailing mat of tiny rounded leaves. It is grown as a warm-season annual outside the mildest climates, blooming continuously from spring through fall as long as moisture is consistent. Plant in partial sun with some afternoon shade in hot climates, since full, intense sun can stress and scorch the fine foliage. Keep soil evenly moist and feed lightly through the season to sustain its long, nonstop bloom.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container stock in fall into humus-rich, well-drained soil in a sheltered spot with some afternoon shade, and avoid disturbing the roots once sited.

directions: Nepalese paper daphne is the Himalayan wild-type species behind the fragrant named garden cultivars already grown for their intensely sweet midwinter flowers, producing clusters of pink-to-white blooms on bare or lightly leaved stems in the coldest months. In its wild form it ranges from fully evergreen to deciduous depending on provenance and winter severity at the growing site. Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil in a sheltered location with morning sun and afternoon shade, since hot afternoon exposure and waterlogged roots are its main causes of decline. It resents being moved once established, so choose the planting site carefully and mulch to keep roots cool and evenly moist.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into moist, humus-rich soil in shade to partial shade, and give it room since it spreads steadily by rhizome.

directions: Broadleaf sedge is the East Asian wild-type species behind the several variegated named cultivars already grown as ornamental groundcovers, distinguished from most Carex by unusually wide, lance-shaped, plain green leaves that look more like a woodland grass than a typical fine-textured sedge. It spreads at a steady clip by creeping rhizomes to form a dense, deciduous groundcover beneath trees and shrubs. Plant in shade to partial shade in consistently moist, humus-rich soil, where it will fill in a shaded bed faster than most clump-forming sedges. Divide in spring if a planting needs to be thinned or propagated.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring into well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, and water regularly the first season to establish.

directions: New Zealand hair sedge is the wild-type species behind the bronze- and silver-toned named selections already popular in containers and borders, forming a fine, hair-like, arching mound of thread-thin leaves in a soft green to bronze-green color. It is evergreen in mild climates and provides fine textural contrast against broader-leaved perennials in a mixed border or container planting. Plant in full sun to light shade on well-drained soil, and provide some afternoon shade in hot inland climates to prevent leaf scorch. It is only moderately cold hardy, so gardeners in colder zones often grow it as a container annual or overwinter it indoors.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox
